title: Acharei Mot: the goat to Azazel (Leviticus 16:21–22)
hookLine: wrongs are confessed over a goat sent into the wilderness

lines: THE ONE WHO TAKES THE BLAME.
TWO GOATS, AS ALIKE AS POSSIBLE.
ONE FOR GOD, ONE FOR AZAZEL.
cards: Scapegoat. In English it's the one who takes the blame for everybody: the intern blamed for the server crash, the kid blamed for the broken lamp. It's become a word for unfairness.
But it started as something else entirely, in Leviticus 16. On Yom Kippur, two goats stand before the high priest, as alike as possible, the rabbis said, in look, in size, in price. Lots are drawn.
One is marked for God. And the other is marked with a word nobody has ever fully explained.

teach.b: The high priest lays both hands on the head of the living goat and confesses over it all the wrongs of the people.
Then a man appointed for the job leads it into the wilderness, carrying those wrongs, the text says, to a land cut off. The lot says: for Azazel. What is Azazel?

teach.h: AZAZEL: A CLIFF, OR A NAME?
teach.b: The Talmud reads it as the name of a place, the hardest, steepest of mountains, a cliff, and Rashi follows that. Others, ancient and modern, read it as the name of a wilderness being.
Commentators have argued about it ever since, and the text doesn't settle it.
And scapegoat? When William Tyndale put the Torah into English in 1530, he read the Hebrew as ez ozel, the goat that goes away, and wrote scapegoat: the goat that escapes.
So the English word comes from one translator's reading of a puzzle.

The Mishnah describes a crimson thread tied to the goat, and records a tradition that when the goat reached the wilderness, a crimson thread tied at the sanctuary turned white, and the people took it as a sign of forgiveness.
Notice what the ritual is not. Nobody blames the goat. It isn't punished for being bad.
It's a vehicle: the wrongs are named out loud, then carried far away.

how: The goat ritual ended with the Temple; on Yom Kippur the Avodah service retells it, and on Rosh Hashanah many Jews practice tashlich, saying verses beside flowing water, and some cast crumbs into it, as a picture of sending wrongs away.

games.q: you're the high priest. the lots are drawn, and the second goat stands before you. what do you do?
o: offer it on the altar too.
lay both hands on it and confess the people's wrongs.
set it free in the camp.
games.why: both hands on its head, the wrongs confessed aloud, then it's led into the wilderness, to Azazel.

practice: Think of one thing you've done that you're still carrying: not your whole life, one thing.
Write it on a scrap of paper in a few plain words, the way the high priest named the wrongs out loud, read it once, then tear it up small and throw it away.
Tomorrow comes what tearing it up can't do; for today, let it go into the wilderness.

wordCard.voice: Azazel. The mysterious destination of the second goat on Yom Kippur, carrying the people's wrongs into the wilderness. A cliff, or a name: the sources differ.

orig.note: Hebrew: the word on the second goat's lot (Leviticus 16:8). its meaning is debated.

carryVoice: Your line: send it away. The wrongs are named out loud, then carried off. See you tomorrow.
